learn/clips: A reward model learns from people's picks, and people's time is scarce. In 2017, Paul Christiano and colleagues showed people pairs of clips of a simulated robot, each a second or two long, and asked which they preferred.
learn/flip: Their reward model learned from those picks with the loss from before. From only nine hundred picks, made in under an hour, the robot learned to do backflips.
learn/train: Training a model means changing it, step by step, so that its loss goes down. So what does one pick do to the two scores?
learn/curve: Here is that loss, against the gap between the winner's score and the loser's. Call the gap z.
learn/right: A pair the model already ranks right, by a gap of three, sits where the curve is nearly flat: little slope, so little to learn.
learn/wrong: A pair it ranks wrong, by two, sits where the curve is steep: a big slope, so a big push. How big, exactly? Walk back through the loss.
back/graph: Draw the loss as a graph. The two scores meet at a subtract node, which makes the gap, z.
back/chain: z goes into a sigmoid node, and a minus ln node turns that into the loss, L.
back/fwd: Run it forward on the pair from before, scored two and one: z is one. As before, sigma is about zero point seven three, and the loss about zero point three one.
back/ln: Now walk back from L, one local slope at a time. Minus ln has slope minus one over its input: at zero point seven three, about minus one point three seven.
back/sig: The sigmoid's local slope is sigma times one minus sigma: zero point seven three times zero point two seven, about zero point two.
back/times: Times the minus one point three seven arriving from above, z gets about minus zero point two seven.
back/cancel: That is no coincidence. Minus one over sigma, times sigma times one minus sigma: the sigma on top cancels the one below.
back/rule: That leaves minus, one minus sigma: one minus zero point seven three, made negative.
back/win: Last, the subtract node. z rises one for one with the winner's score, so r w gets the same minus zero point two seven.
back/lose: But z falls as the loser's score rises, so r l gets it with the sign flipped: plus zero point two seven.
back/step: Step against those slopes, as with any gradient, and the winner's score rises while the loser's falls, by the same amount.
agree/push: So one pick pushes the two scores apart, each by one minus sigma of the gap. Plot that push against z.
agree/one: The pair from before, ranked right by one, moves each score zero point two seven.
agree/neg: Now say the labeler had picked b. The scores are the same, but z is minus one: the model ranks this pair wrong.
agree/neg2: Sigma of minus one is about zero point two seven, so the push is zero point seven three: nearly three times as big. The slope on r l is plus zero point seven three.
agree/far: A pair ranked right by three moves only about zero point zero five. Still, it moves: sigma never quite reaches one.
agree/most: So the model learns most from the picks it gets wrong, and least from the ones it already agrees with.
